items.title: Bowlby's monotropy claim has been substantially revised
items.claim: John Bowlby's original theory emphasised a single primary attachment figure (typically the mother). What does subsequent evidence suggest?

options.text: Monotropy is fully supported by all evidence

Infants form attachment hierarchies with multiple caregivers (Schaffer & Emerson 1964); fathers, grandparents and consistent non-parental carers can serve as attachment figures; quality matters more than exclusivity
Only mothers can be attachment figures

items.reveal:
Schaffer and Emerson's 1964 Glasgow study followed 60 babies and found by 18 months most had multiple attachments; nearly a third had primary attachment to someone other than the mother. Lamb's (2010) reviews of father involvement showed independent contributions to child outcomes.

The monotropy claim, alongside Bowlby's earlier ideas about 'maternal deprivation', shaped 1950s-60s policy (working mothers, daycare, hospital visiting). Rutter's 'Maternal Deprivation Reassessed' (1972) sharpened the distinction between privation (no attachment formed) and deprivation (loss of formed attachment).
items.why: Theories with policy implications need re-examination as evidence accumulates. Bowlby's core insight (attachment relationships matter) survives; the specific claim of monotropy has been substantially revised.

items.title: HM could form new procedural but not episodic memories
items.claim: Henry Molaison (HM) had bilateral medial temporal lobe resection in 1953 for severe epilepsy. After the operation:

options.text: He had no memory of any kind
He could not form new conscious (declarative) memories but could acquire procedural skills like mirror-tracing — improving with practice while denying ever having done the task
He recovered fully within a year
He became a famous psychologist himself

items.reveal:
Brenda Milner began studying HM in 1955. Her 1962 paper documented procedural learning despite dense anterograde amnesia. HM died in 2008; his identity was revealed posthumously. His brain was sliced into 2,401 sections (Annese et al. 2014) and photographed, available online.

His case established that medial temporal lobe (especially hippocampus) is essential for new declarative memory formation but not for procedural learning. Suzanne Corkin worked with HM for 46 years.
items.why: Single-case neuropsychology can produce findings that constrain theories of normal cognition for generations. The dissociation between memory systems was visible in one patient.

items.title: Re-evaluating Stanford Prison
items.claim: Philip Zimbardo's 1971 Stanford Prison Experiment is often cited as proof that situations dictate behaviour. What did later archival work by Le Texier and others reveal?

options.text: Guards received explicit coaching, undermining the 'natural' interpretation
No participant played the guard role

items.reveal_title: Guards were coached, not spontaneously behaving
items.reveal:
Le Texier's 2018 archival analysis and a 2019 American Psychologist article showed guards received briefings encouraging tough behaviour.

The BBC Prison Study (Reicher & Haslam, 2006) produced very different dynamics under similar setup.
items.why: Replication and archival work reshape how landmark findings are interpreted.
